stem: An enterprise CMDB tracks servers, laptops, network devices, and licensed applications, but not API keys, signing certificates, cloud automation identities, fine-tuned AI models, proprietary detection rules, or externally hosted domain names. Several of these assets have no named owner and expired credentials are discovered only after outages. What is the BEST asset-management improvement?
decision_point: extend asset inventory and lifecycle ownership to security-relevant intangible and logical assets rather than limiting governance to physical devices and installed software
misconceptions: only physical devices belong in asset inventories
cloud identities need no owner because the provider hosts them
logical assets can be governed only through incident response

originality.authoring_note: Sibling of the released ephemeral-cloud inventory scenario, but tests inclusion and lifecycle ownership of intangible security assets rather than short-lived compute resources.

options: Keep the CMDB limited to physical equipment because intangible items cannot be inventoried reliably

Define inventory scope to include material logical and intangible assets, assign accountable owners, automate discovery/lifecycle data where feasible, track dependencies and expiration or rotation dates, and reconcile these records with operational systems
List only expired credentials after they cause an outage because active secrets should never appear in any inventory metadata
Treat every cloud-hosted logical asset as owned by the cloud provider regardless of who creates or uses it
explanation: Asset management should cover security-relevant information, logical, and intangible assets as well as hardware. Ownership and lifecycle metadata enable renewal, rotation, protection, dependency management, and accountable disposition without necessarily storing secret values themselves.
distractor_rationales: A hardware-only inventory misses logical assets whose compromise or expiration can create major business and security impact.

Asset management should cover security-relevant information, logical, and intangible assets as well as hardware. Ownership and lifecycle metadata enable renewal, rotation, protection, dependency management, and accountable disposition without necessarily storing secret values themselves.
Inventory can track identifiers, owners, purpose, and lifecycle metadata without exposing secret material, and waiting for outages is reactive.
Provider infrastructure ownership does not transfer business accountability for tenant-created identities, models, certificates, domains, or other logical assets.

stem: A development organization wants to acquire a SaaS platform that will host source code, build artifacts, AI-assisted code generation, and deployment credentials. Procurement proposes accepting the vendor's audit report as sufficient assurance and signing the standard contract without examining data use, tenant isolation, integrations, incident duties, or exit options. What is the BEST acquisition approach?
decision_point: evaluate the service against security, data, integration, shared-responsibility, contractual, supply-chain, and exit requirements rather than relying on one assurance report
misconceptions: a third-party audit report transfers all security responsibility
standard contracts automatically meet organizational requirements
exit and portability matter only after termination begins

originality.authoring_note: Original software/service acquisition scenario focused on SaaS development-platform assurance, shared responsibility, data use, integrations, credentials, and exit planning.

options: Accept the audit report as complete proof and avoid adding organization-specific security requirements to the contract

Assess the platform against defined security and privacy requirements, shared-responsibility boundaries, data and AI-use terms, tenant/isolation and identity controls, integrations and credential handling, incident and evidence obligations, supplier assurance, service levels, portability and secure exit, then contract for required controls and monitoring
Use the service without a contract because cloud providers are responsible for all hosted security
Evaluate only subscription price and developer productivity because source code is already backed up elsewhere
explanation: Third-party assurance reports are useful evidence but do not establish that a service fits the organization's specific security, data, identity, integration, contractual, and lifecycle requirements. Acquisition should address those responsibilities before sensitive development assets are committed.
distractor_rationales: An audit report has a defined scope and period and does not replace evaluation of organization-specific use, integrations, responsibilities, and contract terms.

Third-party assurance reports are useful evidence but do not establish that a service fits the organization's specific security, data, identity, integration, contractual, and lifecycle requirements. Acquisition should address those responsibilities before sensitive development assets are committed.
Cloud services operate under shared responsibility and still require contractual and tenant-side controls.
Backup does not address confidentiality, credential exposure, supply-chain access, data use, or exit and incident obligations.

stem: An enterprise policy states that privileged remote access must use strong authentication. The current security standard requires phishing-resistant MFA for administrators, but an old help-desk procedure still instructs staff to provision password-only VPN accounts for emergency support. Which action is BEST?
decision_point: update lower-level procedures to implement the current mandatory standard and policy, with governed exception handling rather than letting an obsolete procedure override them
misconceptions: an old procedure overrides a newer mandatory standard
policy wording alone is enough without implementable procedures
guidelines and standards have identical mandatory force

originality.authoring_note: Original governance-document hierarchy scenario focused on resolving drift between policy, mandatory standard, and obsolete operating procedure.

options: Follow the old procedure because procedures are always more authoritative than policies and standards

Update the emergency-support procedure so it implements the current policy and mandatory standard, train affected staff, control the document version, and route any true exception through the authorized risk/exception process
Delete the policy because the procedure is more detailed
Reclassify the mandatory standard as an optional guideline so the old procedure can remain unchanged
explanation: Policies set direction, standards establish mandatory requirements, and procedures describe how to perform work consistently with them. Lower-level operating instructions should be maintained so they do not contradict current governing requirements.
distractor_rationales: Operational detail does not give an obsolete procedure authority to override current mandatory governance requirements.

Policies set direction, standards establish mandatory requirements, and procedures describe how to perform work consistently with them. Lower-level operating instructions should be maintained so they do not contradict current governing requirements.
Removing the governing policy avoids rather than resolves the control-document inconsistency.
Changing a requirement's status merely to preserve an outdated process weakens governance without a risk-based rationale.

stem: A safety-critical platform is built from components that each pass their individual security tests. During system integration, however, identity attributes are transformed differently across two services, causing a high-privilege workflow to violate an approved separation-of-duties requirement. The project has no traceability from the original security requirement through architecture, interfaces, integration tests, and deployment acceptance. What is the BEST lifecycle improvement?
decision_point: maintain security-requirement traceability through architecture and integration verification so system-level properties are validated across component boundaries before acceptance
misconceptions: component test success proves system security properties
integration security can be deferred until operations
requirements traceability is only project-management documentation

originality.authoring_note: Sibling of the released architecture-retirement scenario, but tests end-to-end security-requirement traceability and integration validation during development/transition rather than dependency closure at retirement.

options: Accept the platform because every component passed its individual security test

Maintain traceability from approved security requirements to architecture decisions, interface contracts, implementation controls, integration/system tests, acceptance evidence, and later lifecycle changes; add system-level validation of cross-component properties before deployment
Remove the separation-of-duties requirement because integration made it difficult to test
Test the identity transformation only after production deployment when real privileged users exercise it
explanation: Security properties can fail at component boundaries even when each component passes in isolation. Lifecycle traceability and system-level verification connect stakeholder requirements to architecture, implementation, integration, acceptance, and later change so cross-system properties are not lost.
distractor_rationales: Component assurance does not prove that interfaces preserve identity, authorization, trust, or other system-level properties.

Security properties can fail at component boundaries even when each component passes in isolation. Lifecycle traceability and system-level verification connect stakeholder requirements to architecture, implementation, integration, acceptance, and later change so cross-system properties are not lost.
Difficulty of integration does not justify discarding an approved safety or security requirement without proper governance.
Production is too late to discover a known high-privilege integration condition that can be validated before acceptance.
